It is the pleasure of the Board of Directors of the YoMoCeAe of 
Montreal to submit this 105th Annual Report to its many members 
and friends whose interest and support make it possible for the 


Association to carry on its important work in greater Montreale 


There are now eleven branches including Sir George Williams 
College and Schoolse All branches have held individual Annual 
Meetings when detailed reports were given their members and 
friends.e These reports are included in the records of each 
branch. In the case of Sir George Williams College and Schools, 
the Annual Report of the Principal was presented to the Corpor- 


ation of the College. 


The present report deals with matters of general interest and 


concern to the Metropolitan Associatione

METROPOLITAN ORGANIZATION 

There are eleven branches of the Young Men's Christian Association 
in Montreal including its educational branch Sir George Williams 
College and Schoolse While the Montreal Association is under the 
general direction of the Metropolitan Board of Directors, each 
branch is governed by a Board of Management and serves a specific 
area of greater Montreale The Central Branch which is in the 
heart of Montreal's business section draws it's members from all 
parts of the city. The Sir George Williams College and Schools 


is under the direction of a Board of Governors. 


Central Branch ~ 1441 Drummond Street - "Drummond Stanley Building" 


has extensive facilities for physical activities, club rooms, social 
area, food service and a residence which can accommodate 540 meno 
This branch conducted extension units at Strathearn and Devonshire 
Schools, Valois and St. Lambert in 1956. 


NOTE: 20,000 square feet of space in Central building are used 
for offices and classrooms by the evening Elementary and 
High Schools, the Business School and the School of Retail~ 
inge The physical and social facilities are also used by 
the Collegeg while the Drummond, Stanley and College 
buildings are closely integrated using a central heating 
plant and acommon maintenance staff for purposes of 
economy and efficiency. 


International Branch = 5550 Park Avenue = with physical program 


facilities, club rooms, and men's residence: serves Outremont, Park 
Extension, Park and Papineau and the area from Mount Royal to Back 
Rivere It is also the center for an extensive program for various 


New Canadian Groups coming from all parts of the city. 


PAGE TWO 


Lachine Branch - $955 Provost Street, Lachine - a modern “Community 
type" building with administrative offices, club rooms, lounge and 
auditoriums This building is used for leadership training, adult 
program and as Service headquarters of small club groups for boys 


and girls meeting in homes and schools throughout Lachine and Dorval. 


Lakeshore Branch = 278 Lakeshore Road, Pointe Claire = this newest 
Branch of the Montreal Association was established in September to 
serve Beaurepaire, Beaconsfield, Baie d*Urfee, Cedar Park Heights, 
Lakeside Heights, Pointe Claire, and Valoise Use is made of rented 
office space for administrative purposes, while schools, churches and 


homes are used for organized club programse 


Montreal East Branch ~ 122 St. Cyr Street, Montreal East = has Branch 
office and club rooms in the Montreal East Protestant School. Use is 
also made of the School gymnasium, lockers, and showerse For summer 
program the pool at the Canadian Army Ordinance Depot is used for 
swimming programe This Branch conducts an extensive program in the 


Montreal East, Champlain Village and Tetreaultville areas. 


Northeastern Branch <- 5001 Rosemount Blvd. = operates from rented 
headquarters in the Nesbitt School, where there are offices, gymnasium, 
game facilities and club rooms. The Branch carries on a decentralized 
program based on small club groups, which meet in homes and schoolse 
This Branch uses the following Schools to supplement it's area program: 
Drummond, Mountrose, Maple Hill, Nesbitt, Ogilvie, Sarah Maxwell, and 


Rosemount Higho 


PAGE THREE 


Northmount Branch ~- 1455 Rochon Street, St» Laurent - operates from 
a “community type" building similar to Lachine and serves Ville Sto 
Laurent, Cartierville and the Town of Mount Royal with an extensive 
Adult and Youth program consisting of interest groups, clubs and 


physical activities. 


Notre Dame de Grace Branch = 4335 Hampton Avenue - especially equipped 
with gymnasium, recreational and swimming facilities to accommodate 
family activitiese This Branch has a large outdoor area which is used 
for such activities as archery, football, touch-rugby, softball, and 
lacrossee It also has three tennis courts and is used extensively for 


activities in the summer program of the Youth department. 


Southwestern Branch = 1000 Gordon Avenue, Verdun = a pioneer in program 
with a family emphasis, operates a building with social, physical edu- 
cation and swimming facilitiese It has also extended it*s work into 


Cote St. Paul, Crawford Park and Ville La Salle. 


Westmount Branch = 4585 Sherbrooke Street, West = located in the 
residential section of the City of Westmount is equipped with gymnasium, 
pool, residence and social areae It operates a full physical and social 


program for all age groupsoe 


Sir George Williams College and Schools =- 1435 Drummond Street ~ adjoining 
the Central Branch is a modern five storey building opened in 1956. This 
building which stretches from Drummond to Stanley Streets, houses admin- 
istrative offices, classrooms, science laboratories, an auditorium, book 


store, students common rooms, and Student Council offices. 


PAGE FOUR 


Camp Otoreke - Ste. Adolphe de Howard, Quebec = established in 1892 
at Lake St. Joseph, sixty-five miles north of Montreal, is an Island 


Camp for Young Adultse This camp property is owned by the YoMoCeAe 


Kamp Kanawana ~- Stes Sauveur des Monts, Quebec = isa sixty acre 
site of woodland and lakes with a beautiful hillside Summer Vacation 
Camp for boys 8 = 16 years of ageo This property which is near Sto 
Sauveur, about fifty miles from the city is owned by the YoMeCeAo of 


Montrealo 


Camp Perrot - Ile Perrot, North, Quebec - is a summer holiday camp 
for boys and girls 9 - 15 years, of forty-five acres located on 
Ile Perrot about twenty-five miles west of Montreale This property 


is also owned by the Montreal YeMeCeAe 


Christieville Ski Lodge - Christieville, Quebec - is a winter ski 
camp with two lodges for Young Adults located about fifty miles north 


of Montreale This is also the property of the YoMeCoAe of Montreale

Program Modernization and Evaluatione At a two day Conference in 
April 1955, the Secretarial Staff initiated a re-study of the 
objectives of our programe It was proposed that all program should 
help to establish "Values for Living" and that it should “provide 
an opportunity for individuals to grow to maturity and to enrich 
their lives in the following respects - 

le Physical Health 

20 Intellectual Competence and Integrity 

Se Emotional Stability 

4e Sociability 

5e Moral Responsibility 

6e Spiritual Vitalityo® 
As a result of this proposal, 1956 has been a year of constant pro- 
gram examination and evaluation, with a view to relating all YeMeCeAc 
activities to this fundamental purpose. During the year the Metro- 
politan Board of Directors approved a “Three Year Plan of Advance" 
which is directed toward improving the quality of our program and 


services, and expanding the services of the Association to 50% more 


people in the next three years. 1956 saw some great strides made 


in this direction with an increase of 20.4 per cent in membershipe 


Staff Development. Since staff development is an important part of 
the Modernization Project, a policy has been proposed to help staff 
members in many ways;within its framework,workshops in Adult program, 
Youth work, and Physical programs have been held by the Staff of the 
Montreal Association. Regular Staff Meetings in the branches, World 
Service Workshops, City-Wide Staff Meetings and an orientation pro- 
gram for new people joining the staff have all proven helpful during 


the yearo 


PAGE SIX 


CLUBS AND GROUPS 

The value ot small clubs and groups to accomplish the purposes 

of the YeMeCeoAe in its work with people has been recognized and 

used to an increasing degree during 1956, which has been a year 

of encouraging growth in this areas These Clubs direct their own 
affairs and are responsible for their own programs within the limits 

of their capacity and maturity, under Volunteer Leaders and Counsellors. 
This provides a well rounded experience in a democratic setting. The 
programs consist of discussions, debates, speakers on topics of import- 
ance to youth, social, recreational, and competitive sports, and 
service projects in their communitiese tnrollment in such groups 
provides opportunity for personal development and growthe There have 
been increases of 153 groups over last years total of 1,011 to 1,164. 
Enrollment has gone up from 25,041 to 35,096 with the aggregate 


attendance increasing -- by over 70%.

CAMPING PROGRAM 

Kamp Kanawana - The process of adapting the "Values for Living" 
developed by the Montreal YeMeUeAo as the goal of all program, 

into a camp setting, became the prime focus of the Camp Staff this 
past summer. All program was evaluated in terms of its effectiveness 
in assisting the camper grow toward these goalse The Camp Staff, 
under the direction of the Camp Director was trained to use the 
newest and best skilis of supervision in guiding group experience 

to help boys achieve Physical Health, Intellectual Competence and 
Integrity, Kmotional Stability, Sociability, Moral Responsibility, 


and Spiritual Vitality. 


PAGE SEVEN 


Kamp Kanawana - continued 

The personal identification of Staff members with these goals and 
the accentuated interest in the causes of each individual boy's 
behaviour gave some indication of the success of the venture. 
Program took on a more vital meaning even to the Jynior Counsellor 
when it was related in this way to the interests and needs of the 


individual boy. 


The camp once again ran to capacity registration with 523 boys 
attending for an average stay of 3el weekse 
There was an evident increase of interest on the part of older 


boys and many exploration canoe trips were sent into many new 
areas searching for an older boy's rendezvous away from the regular 
Camp sitee The need for such a site becomes apparent with three 
canoe trips per week being transported to areas where chains of 


lakes and rivers permit extended tripping expeditions. 


Camp Perrot - 196 different boys attended during the six week 
camping period for boys, while 98 girls were present for the two 
week period offered to girlse Staff of both camps were of a high 
order with competent leadershipe The original purpose of this 
camp was to provide a short term camping experience for boys and 
girls at a low cost} for this reason, fees for short term campers 
remained at a modest figure, but were raised considerably for 
those staying beyond a two week periode The Foremen's Club and 
the Verdun Y's Men's Club, as a service project, made available 
camping holidays for 24 boys and girls, with Welfare Agencies 
such as the Children's Service Centre sending an additional 18. 
The Camp site was used by various city branches to supplement 


their summer program, three times each weeke 


PAGE EIGHT 


Fun Clubs for Boys and Girls =- are becoming increasingly more 
popular in Montreale Sixteen such Clubs were operated by the 
various “y™ branches in 1956 during July and August with a total 
attendance of 30,834 which was 10,2735 over the previous yeare 
This program provides boys and girls who live in the city with 

a five day a week program of picnics, swimming, crafts, family 
events, competitiveand recreational games and tours of industrial 
plants 

It is significant that these Clubs operate during the summer when 


most organized programs for boys and girls are closed downe 


Camp Otoreke - YeMeCoAe Summer Camp for Young Adults, which is 

used by many young people for part or all of their summer vacations, 
as wel]. as on weekends. 1,088 campers attended the camp during the 
year, thus enjoying a rich experience in a real camping situatione 
The informal program consists of many social and recreational act- 
ivities inand around the camp area: all day outings, evening camp- 
fires, carnivals and tournaments. Religious Services are conducted 
each Sunday morning in the out-door Chapele 

Because of the Camp's location canoeing is very popular, and during 
the summer many over-night canoe trips were made through the northern 
territory. | 

The success of this camping program is due in no small measure to 
the continuing relationship of Mre and Mrse Code McGerrigle, who 
have been associated with this important undertaking for twenty- 

one yearse Mre and Mrse "Mac" have a deep interest in young people 
and this interest has found a ready response on the part of hundreds 


of young men and women over the yearse 


PAGE NINE 


Camp Otoreke =~ continued 


In 1956 the Camp acquired an additional ninety acres, which is on 
the mainland opposite the Otoreke landing. 
The Camp Committee is considering the use of this property to expand 


its program to include family camping. 


ChristievilleSki Lodge - The Otoreke Ski Club had a regord member- 
ship of 163 during the skiing season of 1956 with a full camp of 88 
enthusiastic Young Adults attending the Christieville Ski Lodge on 
good weekendse This lodge provides skiing facilities to groups and 
individuals of the Montreal Association, and to those from other 
parts of Canada, as well as the UcSeAo It has become quite popular 
with new Canadians. The program consists of skiing instruction, 
cross country trips and downhill skiing, besides this an indoor 
evening program of a social nature is planned and operated by the 
Campers, and on Sunday mornings, a Worship Service is conducted at 
the lodge. 

Apart from the winter use of these facilities, they are also used 
by the Montreal Association for various conferences and branch 
staff meetingse During the summer the Friendly Home for Orphans 
uses this Christieville site to conduct a Children's Summer Campe 


IMFORMAL EDUCATION 

The many and varied informal YeMeCoAe activities oerried on under 
specialists in their various fields have an important influence 

on the total program impacte Falling in this category were ballet, 
o41 painting, auto mechanics, photography, wood working, leatheroraft, 


sewing, smooking and others. 


PAGE TEN 
INFORMAL EDUCATION - continued 


Total enrollment in these groups was 2,878 different individuals, 

with total attendance of 46,621, while in other areas of informal 

education such as lectures, forums, study groups, motion pictures 

and television, there was a total attendance of 60,778. Also much 
of educational value is contained in the programs of Youth and 


Adult Clubs. 


The Foremen’s Club = for foremen and supervisors of industry with 

a membership of 531. This Club held monthly meetings with prominent 
guest speakers to address them on topics related to their work, from 
Canada and the United States. It published it's own bulletin. 

Y's Men's Clubs ~ This is the senior men's service club of the YeMceCohe 
of which there are two duly chartered clubs in the Montreal Associations 
the Verdun Y's Men's Club and the Westmount Y's Men*s Club, while a new 
Club was started during the year at the Notre Dame de Grace Branche 
So-Ed Clubs were conducted last year by three of the branches of 

the Montreal Association. These Clubs conducted programs of interest- 
groups, hobbies, lectures, discussions and social recreation for adults. 
English Language Classes continue to be regarded an important service 
to new Canadians by the International Branch, 1,623 different people 
were enrolled in these classes during the year. Many of these people 
knew no English at all and it can be readily understood how important 


this service is in helping them become responsible citizense 


PAGE ELEVEN 


HEALTH AND PHYSICAL FITNESS 

Health and physical fitness continues to be an important part of 
YoMeCoAc program, both for its own sake and for the mental and 
Spiritual development that takes place in a wholesome atmosphere 
of sportsmanship and fair play. 

In 1956 the enrollment in Gymnasium activities was 4,499 

with the total attendance of 28,271 more than doubled that of 


the previous year. 9,712 were enrolled in teams and leagues of 


various competitive sports. 


Swimming Classes - 5,979 individual boys, girls, men and women 


were enrolled in swimming instruction classes during 1956, and 
2,677 tests were given. This swimming program of the YoMoCohe, 
consists of a progression of tests ranging from the begimers 
test through to senior life saving. With the frequency of 
tragic swimming, boating and other accidents which could be 

-, prevented by a better understanding of swimming, it s dangers 
and what to do in emergencies, the YeMceCoAo considers this an 


important part of its program. 


Social Recreation =- There was a total attendance of 81,981 at 

social events during the year. These consist of dances, parlor 
socials, dramatic and musical activities and a variety of trips, 
tours and outingse Many of these events are an integrated part 


of the programs, clubs and groups and have seasonal significance. 


PAGE TWELVE 


SIR GEORGE WILLIAMS COLLEGE AND SCHOOLS 


Extracurricular Activities: 


The large number and variety of extracurricular activities cannot 
be reported in detail. Each of the five units or “Schools® has 
some extracurricular activityo In the College this is naturally 
most extensive in spite of the fact that the greater proportion 

of our students attend in the evening and are, therefore, too busy 
for much extracurricular interest. It is a pleasure to report that 
the YeMeCoAo World Service Campaign was again successful, reaching 
a financial objective of $2,450.00. Some College clubs of the most 
constructive nature are small and receive little recognition, but 
perform a valuable educational servicee In this category is the 
Fellowship Students! Society, composed of those undergraduates who 
are preparing for the YoMoCoAce Secretaryship of whom there were 
thirty-two in the fall of 1956. There is also a newly formed Pre- 
Theological Society, composed of those who expect to enter the 
ministry of the churche 

With the move to the new building, the students of the College 
were able to play host to the National Conference of Canadian 
University Students and the Canadian University Film Conferences 
Our Students also conducted a World University Services display 
which raised some $1,200.00 for scholarshipse Campus clubs 
flourished with some twenty-five day and evenings interest groups 
being active in the Collegeo These clubs brought a number of 
well known public figures to the College as well as providing 


the students with a variety of program. 


PAGE THIRTEEN 
Extracurricular Activities - continued 


The annual Winter Carnival was one of the most successful with the 
College and all the Schools being actively involved. In Athletics, 
the College Teams participated in the Ottawa Ste. Lawrence Inter- 
collegiate Association in Skiing, Swimming, Curling, Basketball, 
Tennis, Soccer, Hockey and Tracke Our Teams played in Ottawa, 
Kingston, New York State, Saint John, NeBo, Quebec City and Lennox- 
ville. Intramural sports also enjoyed a banner year with Fencing, 
Basketball, Volleyball, Rifle, Tennis and Badminton enjoying a high 


degree of popularity. 


BRANCH CHAIRMEN'S COMMITTEE 

This committee, which consists of the Chairman of each of the branches, 
is advisory in nature. It meets periodically by arrangement to discuss 
matters of mutual concern and where appropriate, to offer suggestions 
to branch Board of Management or the Metropolitan Board of Directorse 
During the year, three meetings were helde On one occasion, the 
President of the Metropolitan Board was host at a very enjoyable dinner 
meetings. On other occasions, the meetings were held in the Westmount 
Branch and the Notre Dame de Grace Branche These meetings dealt with 


a progress report on the program modernization project. 


PAGE FOURTEEN 


SIR GEORGE WILLIAMS COLLEGE AND SCHOOLS 


The new erareferred to in last year's report appears to be well under 
waye Classes which were being held in ten separate buildings have been 
consolidated into a new building while retaining some space in the ad- 
joining Central Branch building. 

The new building was formally opened at Special Convocation on April 
6th, and was used for summer classes and came into full use with regis= 
tration for the fall terme 

The Convocation marking the opening of the new building was one of 
three held during the yeare The second was the Annual Convocation 

on May 25th, and the third was a Special Fall Convocation on December 
8the The purpose of the Fall Convocation in 1956 was for students 

who completed their requirements for graduation during the summer 
monthse The School of Retailing, the Business School and the High 


School also held graduating exerciseso. 


Registration 
The total enrollment in the College and Schools for day and evening 


divisions for the academic year of 1955-56 amounted to 6,994 as com- 


pared to 6,678 in the previous year, while an increase of 547 was 


noted in the summer registration. These figures do not include the 


record increase of the 1956 fall registration when the new building 


was brought into full usee

Men's Residence 

The three branches; Central, International and Westmount, showed 

a considerable increase in the use of their men's residence facilities 
in 1956- A total of 204,573 bed nights were recorded for the year, an 
increase of 6,194 over the previous yeare 

Many young men newly arrived in Montreal, find a ready welcome at the 
Central Branch. This Branch is centrally located in the down town 
area. While in Montreal they are kept informed of vaious program 
activities at the “Y" Branches and given a friendly welcome to 


participate. 


Personal Interviews and Counselling 


Individual counselling and interviewing is an important part of the 
daily service of every branch. Many people wishing to talk to an 
understanding person are afforded an opportunity to do soe These 


people come seeking guidance and help with a wide range of problems. 


PAGE SEVENTEEN 


Personal Interviews and Counselling - continued 


Sir George Williams College maintains a full time professional coun=- 
selling servies for its students who are helped by interviews, tests 
and counselling with their many problems including the choice of 
vocations These services provided 56,371 interviews in 1956. 

The College also maintans offices for the part-time use of two inter- 
viewers from the Unemployment Commission. Many situations have arisen 
where the YolleCeAo has been able to help locate jobs for people with- 


out employment. 657 persons were helped in this way last yearo 


PAGE EIGHTEEN 


OUR CHRISTIAN EMPHASIS 


"The YeMeCoAo is a world-wide fellowship of men and boys united 

by a common loyalty to Jesus Christ for the purpose of develop= 

ing Christian personality and building a Christian society" = 

these familiar words, known as the YoMoCeAe purpose as stated 

by the International Cleveland Convention, 1931, continue to be 

the fundamental basis of all the work of the Montreal YoMoCeAc 

Reference has been made in the program section about the steps 

which are being taken to express our basic purpose in a workable 

framework entitled “Values for Livinge" This study and examination 

of methods and tools and the modus operandi of the program does not 

detract or eliminate in any way much that has been done in the past 

but makes possible a more significant performance in the realization 

of goalso 

To delineate the extent to which basic purposes are being realized 

is a task which would defy the wisdom of a cues and yet it is 

definitely known that day by day, the impact (on h hundreds of lives, 
°ear'the progres adding its contribution toward the development 

of Christian personality. Christian emphasis to some is related 

to certain activities - to those however on whom the planning and 

execution of the YoMcCoAe programs rests it is not only specific 

activities but a plus factor permiating all - a motivating force 

behind the entire range of activities which leaves its imprint, 

sometimes readily discernable,at other times in a manner which may 

not be found in overt expression. Formel wership services, devotional 


periods, induction services, religious discussions, camp fire services, 


PAGE NINETEEN 


OUR CHRISTIAN EMPHASIS - continued 


personal interviews, Conferences, Circulation of Week of Prayer 
booklets are typical of the kinds of activity where direct Christian 
emphasis is an integral part of the program. “The Captain’s Chapel" 


in the Central building has been open daily for meditation. 


MEMORIALS COMMITTEE 


This committee, under the Chairmanship of Mr. George Hodge, was 
established several years ago as a Standing Committee of the Metro- 
politan Board of Directors to deal with the proper recognition of 
former officers and leaders of the Association who have rendered 
outstanding service and other memorials that could properly come 
within the scope of the committee's work. During the year, bronze 
plaques recognizing the service of former members of the Montreal 
YeMoCoAo in the first and second World Wars were erected in the 
Central Branch foyere Arrangements were made for suitable brass 
plates to be installed in the new College building recognizing 
special memorial donations of rooms and equipment. 

The committee also gave attention to the recognition of the founders 
of the Montreal YoMoCeAo and in this connection, the names of the 
following were inscribed in the stone walls of the Hall of Remembrance 
leading to the Chapel in the Central Branch: Lay Leaders = George Be 
Muir, Francis Eo Grafton, Te James Claxton, David Bentley, William 
Ge Milne, Edward Te Taylor, CoP. Watson, JeHe Winn, John Holland, 
PoWe Wood, FeHs Marling. Secretarial Leaders - Samuel Massey, 


Alfred Sandhame

The YoMeCoAo’s close relationship with many community organizations 
continued throughout the year, and “"y" facilities were used 2 5416 
times by 651 of these groups. 

The YoMoeCoAo as a member of the Montreal Council of Churches con- 
tinued this active relationship in 1956. It was active in the 
Bryan Green Mission and made available free office space for those 
planning the mission. In some areas regular services were held in 
YoMeC oA buildings by Churches who had no facilities of their owne 
The “Y" continued to carry on its club programs in many of the 
Schools in Montreal through the courtesy of the Montreal Protestant 
School Board. School facilities have also been used for physical 
activities, and social recreation, to supplement the building re~ 
sources of the YoMoCeAe The success of our “Learn to Swim" Campaigns 
were largely due to the cooperation received from the Schools. 

The Montreal Association is also a member of the Montreal Council 
of Social Agencies in which it continued to participate during the 
years It is also affiliated with the Council of Christian Education 
for the Province of Quebece 

Cooperation with the home is an integral part of the YoMoCoAs com- 
munity program. Certain specific activities involving parents and 
their families include family swims, outings, parents nights, 
father-son and mother=daughter programs and panel discussions in 


which parents and youth participated together.

The Annual Financial Campaign was held November 19th to 30th with 

an objective of $221,000., an increase of $11,000. over the pre- 
ceding yeare The experience was good in spite of unusually large 
losses through deaths and removals, and difficulties in some areas 

of getting calls completed within the campaign periode Where care- 
ful appraisals were made and approaches studied, the results amply 
illustrated the desirability of more widespread attention to that 
aspect of the solicitation techniques The final returns showed 
$219,695. from 11,496 contributorse Mre WeSe Kirkpatrick, the 
General Chairman, and Mr. HeMe Mawhinney, Chairman of Special Names, 
both members of the Metropolitan Board of Directors, gave excellent 
leadership to this important undertakings The Sponsors? List numbered 
219 including 8 new names» In addition, 15 laymen rendered excellent 
service as Chairmen of Divisionse The total working force of 1,700 
was well supported by an effective publicity program under the dir- 
ection of Mre Jack Clifforde Dre John Oliver Nelson of Yale University 
Divinity School addressed the opening meeting and in an inspiring 
message, called attention to the problems and frustrations in the 
contemporary "age of anxiety" and pointed out how the YeMeCeAe - 

"the largest lay organization in the world” is meeting the challenge 
of every day needse The usual report meetings were an effective part 
of the campaign technique.

During the year the property at Ste Adolphe de Howard of Mre AeT. 
Syratt adjacent to the holdings used by Camp Otoreke, was acquired 
for the sum of $25,700. with the cost being amortized by the camp 
over a three year period. This property comprises about 90 acres 
and includes a shore line on four lakes with a 170 ft. frontage 

on Lake Ste Joseph, a road frontage of 245 fte, a main frame build- 
ing and a stablee The Otoreke property now has adequate provision 
for parking space and a more comprehensive cemping program, a sub~ 


ject which is currently before the committee.

revenue payments have been received from time to time,was made, and 


the YeMeCeAe received the sum of $6,228. 


PAGE TWENTY-FIVE 


FINANCE AND PROPERTY - continued 


GENERAL FINANCING - 

During the year, endowment investments were liquidated with the 
exception of minimum holdings in a selected list of securities 
with a Wonk value of approximately $8,300. This action was in 
accordance with the policy approved by the Directors of borrow- 
ing from funds within the Association rather than from outside 
sourcese Borrowings were necessary of course to finance the 
final phases of the expansion program launched in 1952. Fortun= 
ately, however, with maximum use of operating funds, payments on 
Capital Fund pledges and loans from the Endowment Funds, it was 
possible to finance all undertakings during the year without 
Bank loans and at the same time to secure maximum earnings on 


temporary surplus cash when available for short periods.

Although World Services occupies a very small proportion of the 
yearly financial budget of our Association, it is a very important 
component of the activities which take place. As someone has said 
in another connection, “if it didn*t exist , it would have to be 
invented.” For World Services is a well-developed, attractive and 
necessary program by which our members and friends are enabled to 
aid and to become interested in people of far-off places who are 

in need of new ideas, new methods. And seldom has a more dramatic 
way been found to demonstrate the values in being generous = the 
benefits, the growth and the response are out of all proportion to 
the efforts expended. 

Since 1889, World Services has been supplying trained YoMcCeAo 
Secretaries from Canada and the United States to assist men and 

boys in other lands throughout the world to become skilled leaders 

of their own peoples. Nearly forty countries in all owe the genesis, 
and sometimes the survival, of their YoM-CeAo movements to the assis- 
tance in men and money, from which established self-governing, self- 
propagating and self-supporting organizations have developed in each. 
Currently 56 fraternal secretaries of the International Committee are 
overseas giving an understanding in democratic procedures to staffs, 
boards and members, which has won the hearty support of governmental 
and educational leaders at all levels. 

One of the gratifying features about support in Montreal for World 
Services has been the ready acceptance year after year of the oppor= 


tunity to extend help to peoples across the world. Our members and 


PAGE THIRTY-ONE 
i Mn ae: aa aa 3 S E RV IC &E § = continued 


friends are often deeply stirred and frequently amazed by visiting 
speakers’ accounts of what is being accomplished with modest app= 
ropriations in money. Such speakers are invaluable in bringing first 
sisal information, not only to our constituency but to a larger aud= 
ience, including boys, girls and young people in High School and 
College classrooms. Over the past several years excellent educational 
work has been done in this manner. 

Last year we were fortunate to have a five-day visit from Nicholas 
Goncharoff, a former member of the Russian army who is now on the 
staff of our International Committee in New York, related to anti- 
Communist works We alsogreatly enjoyed a two-day visit from Paul 
Guinness, the editor of World Communique, while he was returning 

to Geneva from the Far East, after a world-circling tour. 

In 1956 World Services raised a total of $1,486,000.00, Canada’s 


total was $137,300.00. Our local results were as follows:

World's Alliance, the world-wide organization of YeMeCoAo movements, 
with headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, numbers almost as many 
countries( seventy-eight ) in its membership as the United Nations 
has with eighty. The Alliance, which is allocated five per cent of 
our World Service receipts, speaks as the representative body of 
over four million members within 9,000 Associations. It also seeks 
to coordinate experience, methods, personnel, and provides a mediun 
through which the needs across the world can be ascertained and 
world strategy devised. Last October, for example, it was able to 
step into the Hungarian refugee problem in Austria with men and 
material, and to appeal quickly throughout the YMeCeA. World for 
aid to handle its extra burden. 

Its official publication, “World Communique" is probably one of the 
outstanding periodicals of its kind in the world today. A quarterly 
pictorial, which has been for years a stimulating example of how an 
aggressive Christian publication can attract attention and tell a 


story, it comes into more than 500 Montreal homes annuallye

1956 will go down in the records of the 105 years of YeleCeAe 
service in Montreal as a good year, worthy of its predecessors. 
It has included a number of notable accomplishments: the Centen- 
nial building expansion program was brought to a conclusion; the 
registered membership passed the twenty thousand mark for the 
first time; current financial operations improved; the number 
of volunteer Board and Comnittee persons, club and group officers 
and leaders reached an all-time high; the quality of program was 
well mintained onlin many areas improvede These are all “bench 
marks" indicating in a tangible fashion the progress and growth 
of our Association during the year under review. 
In times like the present, our duty as officers and members of 
the Young Men's Christian Association would seem to be quite 
cleare we must see to it that our plans, policies and efforts 
are devoted to providing opportunities and encouragement to people 
to grow and develop into responsible citizens. 
For more than one hundred years, the YelieCeAe has used a simple 
formulae It iss | 

- To give priority to youth in its services. 


- To encourage people to associate with each other in a 
friendly manner. 


- To help many to exercise qualities of leadership. 


- To emphasize the importance of Christian ideals and 
principlese 


PAGE THIRTY-SIX 


This formula has been well tested and has been proven valide 
If we in Canada are to continue to develop and sustain a way 
of life worthy of the present and future Opportunities and 
responsibilities of our country, it will depend on men and 
women of good character. This is the job of the YeoMeCoAcy 


and to this task we must all bend our best effortse

The Young Men's Christian Association of Montreal. 
Montreal, Quebec. 


We have examined the Balance Sheet of the Young Men's Christian 
Association of Montreal as at December 31, 1956 and the related 
Statement of Income and Expenditure for the year ended that dateo 
In connection therewith we made a test examination of the books 

of account and financial records of the Metropolitan Office and 

of the reports from the branches and from the Residence Building 
but we did not make a detailed audit of the transactions of the 
Association for the yeare We have received all the information 
and explanations we have required. 

In our opinion, based on the examination made, the attached Balance 
Sheet and related Statement of Income and Expenditure correctly set 
forth the financial position of the Association as at December 31, 
1956 and the results of its operations for the year ended on that 
date, according to the best of our information and the explanations 


given to us and as shown by the accounting records examined by use 


Pe Ss» ROSS & SONS. 


Chartered Accountants.
